summary: Describes RPCSEC_GSS, a security flavor for ONC RPC that lets RPC-based protocols use the GSS-API for authentication and optional integrity or privacy protection. This makes it possible to plug different security mechanisms underneath RPC services such as NFS.

plainLanguage.summary: RPCSEC_GSS adds a common way for ONC RPC calls to use GSS-API security mechanisms. It can authenticate a caller, detect changes, and encrypt the call data.

what is the rpcsec_gss sequence window
how does rpcsec_gss protect rpc calls
what are the rpcsec_gss service levels
subtitle: A security flavor that lets ONC RPC use GSS-API mechanisms to authenticate and protect calls.

tldr.problem: ONC RPC needed a security method that could provide authentication, integrity and privacy without depending on one security mechanism.
tldr.mechanism: RPCSEC_GSS establishes a GSS-API context, then checks an RPC header and optionally protects call arguments and results. Sequence numbers and a receive window help detect replays.
tldr.outcome: RPC applications can use GSS-API mechanisms without changing the RPC protocol. RFC 2203 is updated by RFC 5403.

today: RFC 2203 is a Proposed Standard published in September 1997. It has been updated by RFC 5403.

sections.title: A Security Flavor for RPC
sections.content:
RFC 2203 defines RPCSEC_GSS, a security flavor for ONC Remote Procedure Call (RPC). It uses the Generic Security Services Application Programming Interface (GSS-API) so RPC can obtain security services independently of the underlying mechanism.

The flavor number is 6. The RFC also adds authentication status values RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM (13) and RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM (14). The protocol is described using XDR, and assumes familiarity with ONC RPC and GSS-API.
sections.plainLanguage: RPCSEC_GSS lets an RPC service use a security mechanism through a shared interface. The RPC protocol can use different mechanisms without defining each one itself.

sections.title: Three Phases and the Credential
sections.content:
An RPCSEC_GSS session has three phases: context creation, data exchange and context destruction. Context creation and destruction use control messages directed to NULLPROC (procedure number zero), rather than to a service procedure.

The credential identifies the control procedure, sequence number, requested service and context handle. Version 1 is defined; version 0 is reserved. The protocol does not negotiate the GSS-API mechanism or quality-of-protection value, so an application using RPCSEC_GSS must specify which combinations it requires.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first establishes a security context, then sends protected RPC calls, and finally asks the server to destroy the context. A credential identifies each call's phase and context.

sections.title: Creating and Destroying a Context
sections.content:
The client begins context creation with RPCSEC_GSS_INIT. If the server replies that more tokens are needed, the client sends another request using RPCSEC_GSS_CONTINUE_INIT. The server returns a context handle that the client uses for later requests.

GSS-API tokens travel in the call data because RPC version 2 limits credential and verifier bodies to 400 octets each, while tokens may be longer than 800 octets. When the client finishes, it sends RPCSEC_GSS_DESTROY with a valid sequence number and header checksum. A server should age out contexts that clients leave behind.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server exchange tokens until the security context is ready. The client later sends a control request to end that context.

sections.title: Three Levels of Data Protection
sections.content:
Each data request includes the context handle and a sequence number. The verifier contains a GSS-API checksum of the RPC header through the credential. The selected service determines how the procedure arguments and results are sent.

  • rpc_gss_svc_none leaves arguments and results unprotected, but the header remains authenticated.
  • rpc_gss_svc_integrity adds a checksum to the arguments and results, along with the sequence number.
  • rpc_gss_svc_privacy encrypts the arguments and results.

The response verifier checks the sequence number of the corresponding request.
sections.plainLanguage: The service can leave the call data visible, protect it against changes, or encrypt it. Even the unprotected-data mode still authenticates the RPC header.

sections.title: The Sequence Window
sections.content:
The server tracks a window of sequence numbers ending at the highest verified number it has seen. It accepts unseen numbers in that window and records them. It silently discards numbers below the window and repeats already received within it.

This allows requests to arrive out of order and lets a client retry after a timeout. The client must use a new sequence number even when retrying the same RPC transaction. The server chooses the window size based on how many requests it expects to process at once.
sections.plainLanguage: The server remembers which recent sequence numbers it has accepted. It ignores a repeated number or one that is too old, which helps prevent a captured call from being reused.

sections.title: Security Limits and Context Errors
sections.content:
Privacy mode encrypts the RPC arguments and results, but leaves the RPC program, version and procedure numbers visible in the header. The RFC notes that these values may be discoverable through rpcbind even without this protocol.

A missing context or failed header checksum can produce RPCSEC_GSS_CREDPROBLEM; stale credentials or an excessive sequence number can produce RPCSEC_GSS_CTXPROBLEM. In either case the client must refresh the context and retry. The RFC also says this protocol does not prevent an attacker from blocking or stealing messages without detection.
sections.plainLanguage: Privacy mode hides the call's arguments and results, not the RPC service identifiers. Some errors mean the client should establish a new context; other errors need to be fixed before retrying.

messages.label: GSS_S_CONTINUE_NEEDED
messages.note: A further token exchange is needed.

messages.label: GSS_S_COMPLETE
messages.note: The next client request begins data exchange.
